cim: Elon Musk Wants to Take AI Beyond Earth
cim_eredeti: Elon Musk Wants to Take AI Beyond Earth
szoveg_eredeti:
For years, the technology industry has focused its efforts on developing tools capable of solving problems that, until recently, depended exclusively on human abilities. However, as artificial intelligence, or AI, gains ground in medicine, education, scientific research, and business, its developers are facing a paradox: The more digital capabilities advance, the greater their dependence on physical resources. For this, Elon Musk talks about Starmind.

Behind a seemingly limitless technology lies an infrastructure that requires electricity, water, land, and cooling systems. Securing these resources under economically competitive conditions has become one of the industry’s greatest challenges.

Elon Musk believes part of the solution could lie beyond Earth. On November 25, 2026, his aerospace company, SpaceX, received conditional authorization from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to deploy up to one million satellites that would operate as data centers in space. The initiative, known as Starmind, aims to harness solar energy available in orbit to meet the growing demand for computing power without relying directly on Earth’s electrical grids.

Following the announcement, Musk celebrated the regulatory approval on his X account, stating that the initiative “will be a great asset for the United States and the world.” His enthusiasm reflects a business vision that extends beyond space exploration and rests on the premise that securing sufficient energy could become just as important as developing better processors. The entrepreneur believes relocating part of the world’s computing infrastructure beyond the planet could reduce the costs of a technology whose expansion is reshaping the energy priorities of major economies.

Although many digital activities are performed on relatively small devices, the operations required to run complex applications take place in facilities that can occupy considerable amounts of land. Data centers house servers and computing equipment that store, process, and distribute information. They are essential both for training artificial intelligence models and for handling requests from millions of people who use these tools. Their continuous operation requires a reliable electricity supply, as well as systems capable of controlling the temperatures generated by electronic components.

The International Energy Agency (IEA), an intergovernmental organization that analyzes developments in global energy markets, estimated that data centers consumed approximately 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, accounting for 1.5% of global demand. Its projections suggest that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, slightly exceeding Japan’s electricity consumption at the time the study was published. While this growth is not exclusively attributable to artificial intelligence, AI is one of its primary drivers.

The issue takes on another dimension when viewed from the perspective of local communities. Building computing facilities can generate investment and employment opportunities, but it also raises questions about who will finance electrical grid expansions and how available resources will be distributed. In regions where water availability is already a concern, the installation of data centers requiring cooling systems creates additional challenges in balancing industrial demands with the needs of local populations.

Against this backdrop, major technology companies have begun venturing into industries that once seemed unrelated to their core businesses. Some are exploring nuclear power, others are establishing agreements with renewable energy producers, and several are investigating alternatives to reduce their dependence on conventional electrical grids. Musk, meanwhile, intends to capitalize on an advantage that sets SpaceX apart from many of its competitors: the ability to manufacture satellites and transport them beyond Earth using its own spacecraft.

In June 2026, Musk advocated for harnessing a much greater proportion of the energy produced by the sun. His argument rests on the idea that orbital facilities could capture solar radiation for longer periods than many terrestrial infrastructures, depending on the satellites’ trajectories. Months earlier, during a conversation with Dwarkesh Patel and John Collison, co-founder of the payment platform Stripe, Musk predicted that “in 36 months, the cheapest place to put AI will be space.” This business forecast has yet to be tested against the actual costs of manufacturing, transporting, and maintaining the necessary equipment.

What SpaceX proposes through Starmind is a fundamental change in the physical location of part of the infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence. Rather than concentrating thousands of processors inside buildings, the company would distribute computing power across satellites operating at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (311 to 623 miles).

These devices would incorporate solar panels to generate electricity and communicate with one another through optical links capable of transmitting information using light signals. The results of computing operations performed in orbit could subsequently be transmitted to Earth through connections with other satellite networks.

Starlink, the connectivity service developed by SpaceX that provides internet access through satellites, would play an important role in this model. Integrating the two initiatives would allow the company to leverage part of its existing communications infrastructure. However, Starmind would serve a different purpose: While Starlink facilitates the transmission of information, the new system would be designed to process it. This distinction is fundamental to understanding why Musk believes his experience in the aerospace industry could give him a competitive advantage in the artificial intelligence market.

In Washington, the proposal is also viewed as an opportunity to strengthen U.S. technological leadership. Brendan Carr, chairman of the FCC, stated on X that Starmind and competing satellite constellations would harness solar energy to “extend America’s leadership in superintelligence.”

His remarks reflect the strategic importance President Donald Trump’s administration places on developing advanced computing capabilities, particularly in an international environment where major economies are competing to master technologies that could transform their industries.

However, the government’s expectations are not shared by everyone in the industry. On March 6, 2026, Amazon, through its satellite communications division, submitted a petition to the FCC requesting that SpaceX’s application be rejected. In the filing, the company argued that the proposal appeared to represent “a lofty ambition rather than an actual plan.”

Amazon questioned the technical information provided and the launch capacity required to build a satellite constellation of such magnitude, suggesting that its deployment could take centuries based on existing launch rates.

Behind this controversy lies a broader commercial rivalry. Amazon is not only developing its own satellite internet network, known as Amazon Leo, but also operates Amazon Web Services (AWS), one of the world’s leading cloud computing providers. A potential reduction in computing costs through orbital infrastructure could reshape the conditions under which these companies market their services.

Google has also identified opportunities in this field and is developing Project Suncatcher, a research initiative aimed at exploring the feasibility of performing artificial intelligence operations using equipment located beyond Earth.
